replying_to: Replying to AID-PURIFIER: A LIGHT AUXILIARY NETWORK FOR BOOSTING ADVERSARIAL DEFENSE
display_title: Official Review of Paper2624 by Reviewer E2aH

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a "purification" scheme to help boost adversarial robustness. Similarly, to concurrent papers like the work by Qian et al. ("Improving model robustness with latent distribution locally and globally", 2021) and Mao et al. ("Adversarial attacks are reversible with natural supervision", 2021), the authors propose to wrap an underlying model with an optimization procedure that "repairs" the inputs given to the underlying model. The method consists of training a network to discriminate between clean and adversarial images (using intermediate activations of the underlying model) and use that discriminator to alter the input during inference to make it "cleaner". The "repairing" process acts as a reverse adversarial attack.
content.main_review:
Overall, the paper is well-written and the text is easy to follow. However, my main concern is that
1) the experimental results are not thorough enough to demonstrate that the method is robust, and
2) a local evaluation of the models on CIFAR-10 did not yield the expected results.

A) Except for SVHN, AID-purifier seems to provide almost no benefits (for the Madry networks, CIFAR-10 goes from 51.64 to 52.65, CIFAR-100 goes from 25.09 to 26.34 and TinyImageNet goes from 20.74 to 21.15). Given the cost of running this inference (10x slowdown for 10 steps of purification), this warrants a discussion.

B) The gap on SVHN seems to come mainly from the difference in clean accuracy (67.39% with purification and 89.20% with). It would be good for the author to explain how AID-purifier improves clean accuracy this drastically on SVHN (the clean accuracy of the Madry trained network seems extremely low). 

C) Under AutoAttack, the SVHN Madry network only drops to 64.36% compared to 49.85% for the evaluation of Table 3. This suggests that more restarts or using more diverse attacks can decrease robustness drastically. Could the gradients be obfuscated? Can the authors plot the loss landscape or use a boundary attack (which does not depend on the model logits)?

D) Finally, I evaluated the Madry et al. + AID-purifier (with 10 steps of purification) CIFAR-10 model using BPDA (Athalye et al., "Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security: Circumventing Defenses to Adversarial Examples", 2018). On a single batch of 128 examples, I was able to find 5 more attackable examples in the AID-purified model (vs the non purified model). Allowing the optimization/purification to move by $\epsilon$ can allow the attacker to move examples as far as $2\epsilon$ away from the original input and can make such models weaker. I might have been unlucky in my evaluation, so I'm willing to discard this result, if the authors can provide more evaluations using more restarts, other black-box attacks and show the loss landscapes.
content.summary_of_the_review: Test-time defenses such as the one proposed in this paper are relevant to the community. However, when proposing such drastic variations, it is important to perform strong evaluations. While this paper was interesting to read, it fails to provide an accurate perspective on the proposed method. In particular, the proposed defense could weaken the defense.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2624 by Reviewer E2aH

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
### A)

Actually, we believe the “worst” column is the most important part of the results.  AID-Purifier can boost the existing adversarial training or purification methods as shown in the Worst column in Table 3: 

46.17->64.14(PixelDefend)->65.61(PixelDefend+AID-Purifier) in SVHN, 

55.32->56.68(PixelDefend)->57.22(PixelDefend+AID-Purifier) in CIFAR-10, 

29.59->30.84(PixelDefend)->33.10(PixelDefend+AID-Purifier) in CIFAR-100, 

26.75->29.82(PixelDefend)->30.48(PixelDefend+AID-Purifier) in TinyImageNet.

The gain is about 2% for CIFAR-10 and about 3.5% for CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet. 

Indeed, the improvements required a slowdown for purification. Less than 10 steps can be used without much performance degradation, though. 

### B)

We didn’t consider the clean accuracy as an important part, because it was always much better than the robust accuracy. But, indeed the clean accuracy for SVHN was drastically improved by purifications. We do not really have an explanation on why this can happen, and we are currently investigating the issue. We appreciate your careful review.

### C)

The experimental results indicate that our method is robust against the attacks that generate adversaries near a decision boundary. For example, in Table 3 and Table 10 of Supplementary material C, DF attack can be as strong as PGD attack for adversarially-trained networks but DF attack can be significantly weakened by purification. This does not happen to PGD attack. Probably this is because the purifiers can easily modify an input example to cross the nearby decision boundary when an attack places its adversarial examples near a decision boundary. This observation is in line with the AutoAttack result in Table 13 of Supplementary material D.4. AutoAttack exploits FAB that minimizes the norm of the perturbation. Thus, we believe our method is more robust against AutoAttack than against PGD, while other defense methods (adversarial training, etc.) are more vulnerable to AutoAttack than to PGD. Thanks a lot for your careful review and insightful comment. We will expand our experiment and discussion on DF and AutoAttack.

### D)

We did not consider BPDA because our discriminator is fully differentiable and there is no need for an approximation. Could you tell us a little bit more on how you generated the BPDA attack? Instead of BPDA, we did evaluate our method under auxiliary-aware attack (strong adaptive attack) to consider the discriminator’s gradient. 
Besides, we are wondering about the details of your experiment result (exact performance).  In Figure 4 of Section 5, we also observed that our method can have more attackable examples (vs. non-purified model) under the auxiliary-aware attack for specific situations. In our case, however, the situation only occurred when the attack concentrated on the auxiliary loss and the overall robust accuracy was actually better when compared to a standard white-box attack (red circle in Figure 4).

---

Overall, we truly appreciate your review, especially on analyzing all the numbers so carefully. In particular, your feedback B and C were tremendously helpful.

content.title: Thank you for the reply
content.comment:
> Actually, we believe the “worst” column is the most important part of the results.

Maybe I misunderstood the table. In Table 3: Madry et al. gets 51.64% and Madry+AID gets 52.65%. While 1% is a reasonably good boost in robustness, it comes at the cost of 10x inference steps. Also note that I am wary of comparing with PixelDefend (which is not a valid defense, see https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.00420.pdf).

> Less than 10 steps can be used without much performance degradation

It would be useful to get those numbers for CIFAR-10. I only see the SVHN numbers in the paper.

> we are currently investigating the issue

Thank you for the taking the concern seriously. I hope the authors can provide an explanation by the end of the rebuttal period.

> We will expand our experiment and discussion on DF and AutoAttack.

Could the authors provide the breakdown from AutoAttack (how many examples are found by Auto-PGD, FAB, Square)?

> We did not consider BPDA because our discriminator is fully differentiable and there is no need for an approximation.

While the optimzation process from AID-purifier is fully differentiable, it is still possible for gradient-based attacks to fail (e.g., non-smooth loss landscapes, un-adapted step sizes, vanishing/exploding gradients). As such, I would recommend the authors to run boundary attacks (e.g., RayS) on a subset of examples (200 should be enough) and compare the results with models without AID-purifier.

For BPDA, one can approximate the backward pass with the underlying non-purified model. As I ran the experiment quickly, I am more than willing to discard my result and will make my final decision based on the authors running a boundary attack.

Overall, I am willing to increase my score, if the authors can:
* Provide an explanation as to why the clean accuracy on SVHN is significantly impacted.
* Provide loss landscapes that show that gradient-based optimization can succeed.
* Can run a boundary attack with enough restarts and queries on a subset of examples (>= 200 to get 0.5% granularity).
* In particular, I'd like to see the results on CIFAR-10 where the clean accuracy of the purified and non-purified models are similar.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for the reply

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
### #1: Provide an explanation as to why the clean accuracy on SVHN is significantly impacted.

For training the main classification network, we have not performed any tuning and instead adopted a set of hyperparameters from a previous work. The setting was originally used for CIFAR-10 in the previous work, and we have used the setting for all of our main network training. The particular choice might have caused the SVHN clean results to have a large variance (SVHN is the only numerical dataset in our experiments).

Another thing to think about is the classification boundaries. The main classification network learns the boundaries of the main classification task. Our auxiliary network learns the boundaries of the adversarial classification task. The two boundaries are related but definitely possess different properties. 

Therefore, it can happen for an adversarial training to cause some of the clean samples to become barely incorrect with respect to the main classification boundaries and be fixed when purified with respect to the adversarial classification boundaries. 

When developing AID-purifier, we have investigated how samples move around the two sets of boundaries when our purification is applied. Based on what we have seen, the above explanation is the most plausible one that we can think of. Showing this with evidence will take some effort, because visualizing/analyzing the boundaries is not a straightforward issue. 

---
### #2: Provide loss landscapes that show that gradient-based optimization can succeed.

To answer your question, we have performed a simple experiment. We have moved an input $x$ from $x_{clean}$ to $x_{adversarial}$  (the adversarial example generated from $x_{clean}$) and observed how the discriminator’s output $p_{adversarial}$ varies. For all the examples that we have checked, the output smoothly increases as $x$ is moved from $x_{clean}$ to $x_{adversarial}$. Certainly, this is not a sufficient test, but it does indicate that the loss landscape of our discriminator is likely to be smooth. 

Another thing to consider is how our purifier works. Our purifier works based on the discriminator’s gradient calculation. So, if the loss landscape is not smooth, our own purification is unlikely to work, either. 

---
### #3: Can run a boundary attack with enough restarts and queries on a subset of examples (>= 200 to get 0.5% granularity).

Following your suggestion, we have evaluated Madry+AID-Purifier/CIFAR-10 using RayS. The results turned out to be 88.15% before purification and 87.64% after purification. There are two things to think about. First, the attack was formed to target the auxiliary network. Because the attack was not targeting the main classification network, the overall performance did not degrade much by the boundary attack. Second, our purifier was not able to improve the defense performance. But, the overall performance is outstanding anyway, because the RayS attack is not being effective overall because it fails to attack the main network. 

We have provided the results for “auxiliary aware PGD attacks” in Figure 4. The performance we have found in the figure is in line with what happens with RayS attack - the overall effect of attack is weak when the attacker focuses on the auxiliary network only; the overall effect of attack can be reduced by our purification when the attacker focuses on the main network only; when the attacker tries to jointly attack the main classifier and the auxiliary network, it is difficult to form a single gradient method that is jointly effective to both networks. In the end, our purification remains useful for all the attacks that we have tried so far.  

---
### #4: In particular, I'd like to see the results on CIFAR-10 where the clean accuracy of the purified and non-purified models are similar.

We are not sure if we understood your feedback well. Did you mean SVHN instead of CIFAR-10? In any case, we hope we have addressed the SVHN clean accuracy issue in our first response above (#1). Related to the issue, there is another thing that you can check out. For SVHN, the clean accuracy is just fine for the adversarial training of Zhang or Lee (the last two of the 4 adversarial training). Nonetheless, AID-purifier provides hefty improvements in robust accuracy for both - for instance, for Zhang/PGD, the robust accuracy of SVHN is improved from 36.72 (without AID-purifier) to 45.73 (with AID-purifier).

content.title: Thank you for the reply
content.comment:
> the output smoothly increases

The authors claim that the loss landscape of the full model (including the 10 optimization steps) is smooth. I also assume that the authors have checked whether gradients are vanishing or exploding. As such, AutoAttack should be able to find an attack close to the optimal (since gradients are informative). Yet, the purified SVHN obtains a robust accuracy of 64.363% against AutoAttack and 49.85% against PGD. Maybe I misunderstood the table.

Second, looking at the code, I see heavy use of `torch.clamp` within the model being evaluated which will prevent gradients from flowing. Can the authors check that gradients are indeed non-zero? Can the authors replace the clamp with a differentiable log-barrier?

> First, the attack was formed to target the auxiliary network. Because the attack was not targeting the main classification network, the overall performance did not degrade much by the boundary attack.

I am not sure I understand the authors comments. Why is the attack not targeting the complete defense?

> Second, our purifier was not able to improve the defense performance.

This seems suspicious to me. When a model is strictly more robust, I'd expect the relative black-box performance to reflect this. Maybe focusing on only 200 examples and doing more restarts and queries than standard RayS would shed some light. Maybe combining Square and RayS to get a more accuracy picture could be helpful here.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a plug-in to improve the model robustness against adversarial attacks. Specifically, different from previous generative purifiers, the proposed method put two layers of features as the input of the discriminator. In addition, an AVmixup data augmentation strategy is proposed to train the discriminator. The experimental results illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

(1) This paper is well-motivated, the proposed method makes sense to me, and the results are reasonably good.

(2) This paper is well-written and easy to understand. I could quickly understand the proposed idea.

(3) The experiments are done on several base methods, and in most cases, the proposed method could improve the results.

Weaknesses:

(1) I suppose Table 3 is under the white-box attack setting. For this table, I suggest reporting the performance under the different numbers of attack steps (eg, 20 steps, 50 steps, 100 steps, or even more, see [a] for detailed test settings) for the PGD attacks. As far as I know, this method could further show the robustness of the defenses. 

[a] Xie, Cihang, et al. "Feature denoising for improving adversarial robustness." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

(2) I am also wondering if there are more details about how to select two layers of the features as the input of the discriminaot.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a reasonable and interesting method, conducts comprehensive experiments to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2624 by Reviewer p83T

content.summary_of_the_paper: The present method is an add-on to an adversarially trained classifier where the present method denoises/purifies the adversarial inputs. The method has shown efficacies when it is used together with PixelDefend (another purifier) method. The methodology seems fast.
content.main_review:
Good idea but the presentation is not good enough:
==============================================
Strengths
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The overall idea seems light-weight w.r.t the other SOTA mentioned in the paper.
2. Presentation is fairly well.
3. Summary of the existing purifiers is shown well. 


Weaknesses
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The Discriminator, D(.): How are we fixing the discriminator architecture, how many seeds are considered to report the result. The proper justification behind the input to the discriminator is not seen. The discriminator considers *only* the layers but one can argue why not the input too? 
2. Comparison w.r.t. baseline: The reviewer finds that the comparison with the baseline SOAP is not very fair. SOAP considers different SOTA architectures to show their efficacies but the present method doesn't - am I missing something?
3. AVmixup procedure: it is not very clear what is the mixup ratio, i.e. the value of $u$? What is the range of $u$, is there any effect on the result if we take different values of $u$?
4. It is evident that the 15th layer by itself can perform well, so why is the methodology considering the 1st layer as an input to $D(.)$ is not very clear. The initial layer of CNN happens to capture edge-like information (generic in nature). Seems like if we consider *only* the 15th layer, i.e. that is the most informative layer IMHO, the present method has very little difference with SOAP-like methods. 
5. Table 3. It appears to the reviewer that the compared methods are a bit old SOTA. Any reason why not any very recent method is not compared.
content.summary_of_the_review: The papers lag a comparison with the recent SOTAs, most of the compared methods are a bit old. The consideration of 1st layer in $D(.)$ is not well motivated and seems like the 1st layer doesn't make any huge difference. Without the 1st layer, the present method is yet another SOAP method.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2624 by Reviewer p83T

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive comments.
1. We fixed the discriminator architecture as a simple fully-connected network because the performance was about the same for more complex networks. The results were generated with one seed, but the overall effectiveness was confirmed to be the same for three different seeds. Lastly, in general, mutual information estimation of high dimensional inputs doesn’t work well. That’s why we only considered the representation layers. 
2. First of all, SOAP is not considered as an add-on in our work because it requires a joint training with the main classification network (this is explained at the end of the first paragraph in p.2). In the SOAP paper, ResNet and Wide-ResNet were considered. Between the two, SOAP performs better with Wide-ResNet. In fact, many of the recent works consider Wide-ResNet only because of the relatively better performance. We followed such previous works.  
3. On the 7th line in Algorithm 1, you can find the range of u. Also, we think we don’t have to tune u considering our purpose as described in Section 3.2.
4. The motivations are elaborated in Section 2.2 and 3.1, and the performance difference reported in Appendix E.2 (Table 15) is not really small - 48.93% vs. 50.10%. Our method and SOAP are both purification methods. Our method, however, is different in many ways including no need for a joint training with the main network (i.e., AID-purifier is an add-on). Aside from the performance, we believe the fundamental design principles of our work are positive contributions to the research community. 
5. Compared to other defense methods, there are few studies on purifiers and even fewer studies on purifiers that are available as an add-on. Thus, to the best of our knowledge, PixelDefend (2018) in Table 3 and NRP (2020)  in Table 10 of the Supplementary material are not recent but still the state-of-the-arts.
